intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 8 units · tectonics to contours

Grade 12 is “geography of Eritrea in depth”. Grade 11 is the toolkit: how the crust moves, how water and wind carve, how people settle, then a first look at Eritrea’s place, relief and contour maps. Read each unit as a *story with a cause* — examiners mark the cause, not only the landform name.

intro_cards.title: Worked contour gradient
body: Two points: 1 200 m and 1 000 m. Map distance between them is 4 cm. Scale 1:50 000 (1 cm = 500 m).
Rise = 200 m. Run = 4 × 500 = 2 000 m. Gradient = 200/2000 = 1 in 10 (or 10%). Write both the fraction and a sentence: “For every 10 m walked horizontally you climb 1 m.”

cards.title: 1.1 Tectonic Plates
body: The earth consists of a rigid outer layer called the lithosphere.
About 250 million years ago, there was a single super continent called Pangaea surrounded by a single super ocean known as Panthalassa.

cards.title: Worked: weathering vs erosion
cards.problem: A granite boulder cracks in place after freeze–thaw. Is that weathering or erosion?

steps.text: Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion moves the pieces.

cards.answer: Weathering (frost action). Erosion starts when water/wind/gravity carries fragments away.

cards.title: Tectonic forces
body: Earth’s plates move; boundaries: divergent, convergent, transform.
Earthquakes & volcanoes cluster at boundaries. Folding/faulting build mountains.

cards.title: Fold mountains
body: Compression at convergent boundaries buckles layers into folds.
Earthquakes release built-up elastic strain.

body: Write one idea students often confuse with this topic, then the correct distinction.

Teaching the difference is better than re-reading the page.

cards.title: 1.3 Folding
body: When plates move towards each other and collide, the compressive forces that are created make the rock layers bend up and down.
Subsequently, the shape of the resulting land form looks like corrugated iron.

questions.q: When the splitting continued, Laurasia was broken into:
why: The textbook: Pangaea first split into Gondwanaland and Laurasia; 'in the northern hemisphere Laurasia split into North America and Eurasia (Europe and Asia)'.
Africa, South America, India and Australia/New Zealand came from Gondwanaland.
